claims.summary: Randomized encryption without an enclave lacks server-side equality search. It is a legitimate choice when the application only stores and retrieves ciphertext without that search requirement, not for this parameterized lookup.

Deterministic Always Encrypted supports equality comparisons on this supported bigint column, with the stated encrypting driver and external keys. It preserves the required client/engine boundary but still reveals equality patterns.
TDE encrypts files, logs and backups at rest while the engine still processes plaintext during authorized queries. It fits a storage-theft requirement, not the specified separation from the engine.
DDM limits returned presentation for readers lacking UNMASK and leaves stored data unchanged. It is useful for accidental display exposure, not keeping plaintext outside the engine.

sourceReviews.supportingSummary: Inspected Configure Always Encrypted, Limitations and Database permissions in the MCP body. Deterministic encryption permits equality point lookups; randomized encryption without enclaves cannot search encrypted columns. The driver encrypts parameters, plaintext keys remain outside the engine, and deterministic ciphertext discloses equality patterns. bigint avoids the documented string-collation requirement; literal comparisons are not substituted for the stipulated parameters.

The actual training text distinguishes file-at-rest TDE from client-side Always Encrypted and explicit server-side column encryption. Its encryption-layer paragraph directly references the cited Always Encrypted article. I use its TDE distinction, not its unqualified suggestion that no Always Encrypted configuration ever processes plaintext in an enclave.

Overview, Permissions and the security note establish that DDM changes query results, not stored values, and is not a cryptographic barrier to the database engine. It is a useful presentation control but cannot satisfy the client-versus-engine encryption requirement.

choiceReviews.rationale: The Always Encrypted article explicitly excludes searching randomized ciphertext without secure enclaves. Randomized encryption is a real choice for stronger pattern concealment when these server-side lookups are unnecessary, or with separately configured supported enclave operations; neither context is this stem.

The documented deterministic mode supports equality point lookups while an enabled client driver encrypts parameters and decrypts results outside the engine. The bigint column, parameterization and external-key access remove the principal type, literal and client prerequisites relevant to this selection. Equality-pattern leakage remains possible.

The encryption unit assigns TDE to files, logs and backups at rest and explicitly says it does not protect against appropriately authorized database users. TDE can preserve normal querying while protecting stolen storage, but that is not exclusion of plaintext from normal engine processing.

The masking article says underlying data is unchanged and masking is applied to query results. DDM fits limiting accidental display exposure to restricted readers; it neither encrypts the bigint values for the engine nor implements the required external-key boundary.

review.verificationNotes: Independently derive B, not a general endorsement of every Always Encrypted deployment. SQL Server 2022 and the no-enclave boundary are explicit; the sources document the applicable released SQL features, not an unknown-maturity methodology. No executable snippet is present; the parameter and type conditions were inspected. The negative-wording warning is necessary to exclude enclave behavior, and 'Always' is a feature name rather than an absolute secrecy promise. Advanced is defensible as a two-constraint protection/query tradeoff: randomized encryption meets the trust boundary but not the lookup, whereas TDE preserves lookup behavior but not that trust boundary. This is the preserved dp800-direct-013 lineage, not a new duplicate; its fact differs from the symmetric-key session prerequisite in d2-001. PASS 2 only.
review.confidenceReason: High confidence in the uniquely supported key from the actual encryption and masking bodies, with the deterministic-pattern limitation retained. This review is source-based, not a claim to have executed an Always Encrypted client.

claims.summary: SELECT enables reading every column but does not itself unmask Phone. Combined with the narrowly scoped Phone UNMASK grant, it supplies precisely the separate access and presentation permissions required.
Table UNMASK would reveal both masked columns once SELECT is granted. That is suitable for a role authorized to see all masked columns on Contact, but too broad for Phone-only disclosure.
SQL Server 2022 supports column-scoped UNMASK. Phone-column UNMASK together with SELECT reveals Phone while leaving Email masked under the explicitly closed permission baseline.
ALTER ANY MASK governs mask administration, with table ALTER additionally required to change definitions. It fits a mask-maintenance task, not reading data with unchanged mask definitions.

sourceReviews.supportingSummary: Inspected Permissions, SQL Server 2022 granular permissions and the column/table UNMASK examples. SELECT supplies table reads; UNMASK is separately scopeable down to a column starting in SQL Server 2022. Table UNMASK is broader, and changing a mask requires ALTER ANY MASK plus table ALTER. The source also excludes a claim of inference-proof secrecy.

choiceReviews.rationale: Permissions states that SELECT on a table permits reading its data; UNMASK by itself does not grant reads. With the stem's closed effective-permission baseline, table SELECT is necessary to read every column while the existing masks remain.

The granular examples distinguish table UNMASK from column UNMASK. At table scope it exposes both Phone and Email once SELECT is granted. It is appropriate when both masked columns may be revealed, not the stipulated Phone-only presentation.

The SQL Server 2022 section expressly permits column-scoped UNMASK and demonstrates GRANT UNMASK ON table(column). Applying that scope to Phone, together with table SELECT, changes Phone presentation without unmasking Email under the explicitly closed permission baseline.

ALTER ANY MASK is for adding, replacing or removing mask definitions, also requiring ALTER on the table. It is useful for a mask-administration role, not a read/unmask grant, and changing definitions is expressly outside this task.

review.verificationNotes: Independently derive the complete two-selection set A,C. The question correctly pins SQL Server 2022 rather than implying granular UNMASK on all historical versions. Its exclusion of inherited grants, DENYs and administrative access is important because CONTROL implies unmasking. Grant descriptions are technically valid; no executable code is claimed tested. Intermediate implementation difficulty fits combining read permission with a narrower presentation permission. The preserved ID is a refresh of its own baseline, not a new item; d2-002 instead concerns values physically copied by a masked reader. No grammar, length or answer-count ambiguity found. PASS 2 only.
review.confidenceReason: High confidence: the product article directly states both permissions, the 2022 scope enhancement and the mask-administration prerequisites; all four choices can be distinguished without assuming hidden grants.

claims.summary: A FILTER predicate controls access to stored rows for SELECT, UPDATE and DELETE. It can hide a newly inserted row from later reads, but does not reject that INSERT merely because the row would be hidden.
BEFORE UPDATE evaluates the old rows targeted for update. It can block changes to already-disallowed rows, not validate the new values of an INSERT.
BEFORE DELETE protects removal of existing rows. It is the appropriate timing for a deletion restriction and is not invoked as the INSERT new-value gate.
AFTER INSERT block predicates reject inserted values that violate the enabled policy. The platform is explicitly SQL Server 2022, avoiding unsupported cross-platform block-predicate assumptions.

sourceReviews.supportingSummary: Inspected Description, predicate behavior and Permissions. Filter predicates govern visible/readable existing rows; INSERT can create rows later filtered from reads. AFTER INSERT block predicates check the inserted values and fail violating writes. BEFORE UPDATE and BEFORE DELETE are separate operation-specific checks. SQL Server is supported; Fabric/Synapse block-predicate parity is not inferred.

choiceReviews.rationale: The source explicitly allows INSERT of a row that a filter will hide during later operations. A FILTER predicate is appropriate for limiting visible existing rows, but does not by itself reject these newly inserted values.

BEFORE UPDATE applies to existing rows targeted for an update. It can prohibit updating a row that currently violates the condition, but INSERT is a different operation with a different predicate event.
BEFORE DELETE can block deletion of existing rows, which is a valid RLS write restriction. It is not fired as the inserted-row check required by this INSERT question.

The article identifies AFTER INSERT as a block-predicate event evaluating the newly inserted row and says violating block operations fail with an error. This is the exact operation and resulting-state check requested.

review.verificationNotes: D is uniquely correct. The stem is mechanism selection, not a complete CREATE SECURITY POLICY script; an operative predicate/policy is implicit in choosing the mechanism, and no unmentioned principal exemption is needed. SQL Server 2022 supports the released RLS behavior first introduced in SQL Server 2016. Beginner/concept-recall is honest for this operation/timing distinction. Before/after alternatives have genuine uses rather than invented features. Preserved baseline lineage is retained, and the policy schema-binding permission diagnosis in d2-003 tests a different fact. PASS 2 only.
review.confidenceReason: High confidence because the RLS product article separately states filter INSERT behavior and all three block-event alternatives; no claim depends on unsupported Fabric write predicates.

claims.summary: TDE protects files at rest and can be useful alongside column encryption. It does not open the existing symmetric key needed by this ENCRYPTBYKEY operation.
An Always Encrypted driver supports client-side column encryption with external keys. This operation deliberately uses server-side ENCRYPTBYKEY and an existing database key instead.

The linked column-encryption examples open the certificate-protected symmetric key before ENCRYPTBYKEY and DECRYPTBYKEY. That supplies the missing step without changing the specified encryption design.
A mask changes returned presentation and can reduce accidental display exposure. It neither opens AccountKey nor performs the specified cryptographic operation.

sourceReviews.supportingSummary: Inspected security prerequisites and both encryption examples. A certificate protects an AES symmetric key, a varbinary column stores ciphertext, and OPEN SYMMETRIC KEY ... DECRYPTION BY CERTIFICATE precedes ENCRYPTBYKEY(KEY_GUID(...), column). The simple example does not require an authenticator argument. This is server-side column encryption, not client-side Always Encrypted.

The training's column-encryption section independently demonstrates opening the certificate-protected key before ENCRYPTBYKEY, then closing it. Its layer comparison assigns TDE to storage and Always Encrypted to a client/engine trust separation, distinguishing the otherwise real alternative controls.

The actual DDM overview says query-result masking does not alter stored values. It supports rejecting a mask as a substitute for opening a cryptographic key, while preserving masking's legitimate display-limiting use.

choiceReviews.rationale: TDE is a real at-rest protection for files and backups, and may coexist with column encryption. Nothing in its documented layer role opens AccountKey for this ENCRYPTBYKEY session; the explicit symmetric-key prerequisite remains unmet.

An Always Encrypted-enabled driver serves client-side encryption using its own key metadata and external key access. The displayed statement instead uses a database symmetric key through ENCRYPTBYKEY; enabling that driver is not the documented OPEN SYMMETRIC KEY step.

Both the product's simple symmetric example and the training place OPEN SYMMETRIC KEY ... DECRYPTION BY CERTIFICATE before ENCRYPTBYKEY. AccountKey exists but is closed, and the protecting certificate is usable in the authorized session, so this is the missing operation.

A mask changes returned presentation for masked readers and does not operate the symmetric key. It is suitable for display exposure reduction, but cannot perform the cryptographic setup required by the shown update.

review.verificationNotes: C is supported. Statically inspected the UPDATE, ENCRYPTBYKEY and KEY_GUID call shape against the actual simple-encryption example. nvarchar(20) plaintext and varbinary(256) destination do not introduce a plausible size/type conflict; existing key/certificate and authorized maintenance conditions avoid repeating creation prerequisites. No SQL execution was performed or runtime error invented. The mandatory wording is specific to this closed key, not every encryption method; 'this session' has a clear referent. Intermediate operational prerequisite selection is appropriate. Distinct from direct-013's client/engine boundary and deterministic lookup choice. PASS 2 only.
review.confidenceReason: High confidence from two inspected encryption bodies and a separately checked masking contrast; source examples directly establish the necessary key-opening order.

claims.summary: The product article says SELECT INTO by a reader without UNMASK writes masked values to the target. Those stored zeroes are not hidden originals, so an authorized re-extraction is needed if real values are legitimately required.
Source UNMASK would let that reader see originals in a fresh authorized source query. It does not retroactively change values already materialized in a different table.
Removing a mask can reveal underlying values when that table actually has a mask over real stored data. Here the copy has no mask definition and its stored data is already the masked output.
Partial masking exposes portions of stored string values; it does not recover information lost during an export and is not the numeric default-mask recovery mechanism.

sourceReviews.supportingSummary: Inspected the default-mask table, Permissions, export/copy behavior and mask removal examples. A numeric default mask returns zero; SELECT INTO by a reader without UNMASK materializes masked data in the destination. Ordinary masking leaves the source unchanged, and changing permission or dropping a mask exposes underlying data only where that data still exists.

choiceReviews.rationale: The documented SELECT INTO/export rule places masked values into the new table. Given that this destination physically holds zeroes and has no mask, its missing originals must come from a new authorized source extraction, not from a presentation-permission change on the copy.

UNMASK with SELECT permits a fresh query to retrieve unmasked source values. The article distinguishes that presentation rule from masked values already materialized in another table; rereading that existing copy does not rerun the extraction or restore lost information.

DROP MASKED is valid for removing a real mask from a column that still stores original data. This question expressly states the copy has no mask definition and stores zeroes, so mask removal cannot reveal originals there.

The product table describes partial masking as a custom string display function, not recovery of numeric values. Even on an eligible string column it can expose only portions of that column's stored value; it cannot reconstruct data lost in the earlier masked copy.

review.verificationNotes: A is uniquely correct given the explicit source/copy state. The export account is authorized to perform the copy, so the question does not confuse SELECT with permission to create a table. Inspected SELECT INTO semantics but no executable script is supplied or claimed run. SQL Server 2022 falls within the documented released masking feature. Advanced troubleshooting is supported by tracing the source presentation into physical destination data and then distinguishing a later permission change from data recovery. The correct option is longer but not materially disproportionate to every alternative; all alternatives address real masking operations. Unlike direct-011, this does not ask which scopes to grant on a live masked table. PASS 2 only.
review.confidenceReason: High confidence from the source's explicit masked-copy rule and the stipulated absence of a destination mask; the recovery conclusion follows from stored values, without claiming DDM encrypts data.

claims.summary: With policy SCHEMABINDING OFF, callers need permissions on predicate dependencies. This can make queries work when direct dependency access is acceptable, but violates the explicit entitlement-table boundary.
A disabled policy does not filter rows. Disabling it can be a controlled diagnostic step, but cannot satisfy continued row-level enforcement.
Broader authority can supply missing access, but also allows policy modification and direct entitlement-table access. It is an administrative solution, not the required least-privilege repair.

The product article states that a schema-bound policy bypasses extra dependency permission checks for queries on the target. With compatible objects and unchanged predicate logic, it preserves filtering without directly granting lookup-table access.

sourceReviews.supportingSummary: Inspected policy SCHEMABINDING behavior and Permissions. With policy binding ON, querying the protected table bypasses additional predicate/dependency permission checks; OFF requires appropriate access to the function and dependencies. An enabled policy still filters dbo/db_owner, although administrators can alter/drop it. Disabling the policy stops its enforcement.

choiceReviews.rationale: Additional SELECT permissions are the documented way to use an unbound policy when direct dependency access is acceptable. Here they grant exactly the sensitive entitlement-table access the stem prohibits, so successful execution alone is not an adequate repair.

The article says disabled predicates do not affect rows. Disabling a policy is a real administrative operation, but with the existing table SELECT it abandons the required continued filtering rather than preserving the authorization boundary.

db_owner supplies broad administrative authority and the ability to alter security policies, rather than narrowly preserving dependency isolation. The source expressly does not say db_owner automatically bypasses enabled row predicates; nevertheless that membership is incompatible with the stated no-direct-entitlement-access boundary.

Restoring policy-level SCHEMABINDING ON removes the extra dependency permission checks while an enabled policy with unchanged predicate logic keeps row filtering. The stem establishes compatible objects, so function-level binding alone is not confused with the policy switch.

review.verificationNotes: D is supported without granting entitlement-table SELECT. Reviewed policy versus function binding separately, and checked that the explanation does not claim owner immunity from RLS or inability of administrators to change it. An authorized controlled recreation is an administrative prerequisite, not permission delegated to readers. The negative wording defines an essential access boundary; pronouns clearly refer to reader queries and predicate dependencies. Advanced diagnosis is reasonable because a function may remain schema-bound while the distinct policy setting changes permission evaluation. Released SQL Server 2022 RLS behavior is evidenced. This differs from direct-012's INSERT timing and baseline direct-004's DDL dependency-protection use of SCHEMABINDING. PASS 2 only.
review.confidenceReason: High confidence from the product article's explicit ON/OFF permission comparison and enabled-policy behavior, including the administrator exception relevant to the distractor.

claims.summary: The source's role-delegation example requires AS role to invoke the role-held grant option. A plain grant works when the executing user has its own appropriate delegation authority, which Mira lacks.
AS selects the recorded grantor and requires authority to use that grantor. Mira's stated authority comes from ProcedureDelegates, not dbo; dbo would fit an independently authorized owner operation.
AS ProcedureDelegates uses the role's grant option, but WITH GRANT OPTION also lets NewReader delegate. That is valid when onward delegation is intended, which this request prohibits.
The documented role-member pattern uses AS role to invoke a role's grant option. Omitting WITH GRANT OPTION on the onward grant gives NewReader execution but not redelegation.

sourceReviews.supportingSummary: Inspected SQL Server GRANT syntax, AS, WITH GRANT OPTION and Permissions. The product's role example explicitly shows a member's plain onward GRANT failing and AS role succeeding. WITH GRANT OPTION separately conveys further delegation; AS identifies the grantor and is not itself a general impersonation permission.

choiceReviews.rationale: The source gives the same permission-chain pattern: a role has grant option, but its member's plain GRANT fails because the member lacks an individual grant option. A plain statement is appropriate for an independently authorized grantor, which Mira is expressly not.

AS selects a grantor whose authority the executing user is allowed to invoke; the Permissions section requires that authority. The stem provides only ProcedureDelegates membership, not authority to use dbo. An owner-authorized grant is a valid different context, not this delegation chain.

AS ProcedureDelegates supplies the role-held authority, but WITH GRANT OPTION also grants onward delegation to NewReader. This is the documented form when delegation is intended, and conflicts with the requested nondelegating result.

The syntax and worked role example support GRANT EXECUTE ... TO NewReader AS ProcedureDelegates. Invoking the role grantor and omitting WITH GRANT OPTION conveys procedure execution without granting additional onward delegation in this statement.

review.verificationNotes: Independently derive D. Statically checked the setup grant and all four candidate statements against the product syntax/example; no database execution was performed. The given role membership and lack of other delegation authority make AS dbo and the plain grant unsuitable. This conveys no guarantee about undisclosed pre-existing NewReader permissions; it correctly addresses whether the requested statement grants delegation. SQL Server 2022 GRANT is a released feature, not an imported Fabric variant. Intermediate implementation difficulty fits a specific grantor-chain rule plus the grant-option exclusion. The pronouns distinguish Mira, role and recipient. Archived direct-099 removes an existing grant option; this item instead exercises AS role for onward granting and is not the same operation. PASS 2 only.
review.confidenceReason: High confidence because the cited GRANT article contains a direct role-member failure/success example and independently defines the two clauses that separate the alternatives.

claims.summary: Direct-grantee rows are useful for auditing explicit grants and denies, but repeating that filter still omits the effective role-derived access that motivated this investigation.
The permissions training explicitly uses fn_my_permissions with OBJECT scope to inspect effective permissions for the current user. That matches both the target object and the no-change requirement.
The principals catalog identifies database identities and principal types. It is appropriate for identity inventory, not a complete effective-permission answer for Sales.Invoice.
sys.masked_columns reports masking definitions. It is appropriate for mask inventory, not determining the current user's effective object permissions.

The actual principal sections identify sys.database_principals as the location of database-principal SID/type/type_desc metadata. This supports the identity-inventory distinction, not an assumption that Azure management RBAC or an identity's type enumerates its effective SQL object permissions.

The training's principals join and the Entra article's sys.database_principals property tables describe database identity metadata. A name/type inventory is legitimate but does not compute the user's effective rights on this particular object.

review.verificationNotes: B is supported and unique. Checked the embedded SQL expression despite this being a single-select rather than code-format record; it matches the actual training's OBJECT-scope invocation. This is related to archived direct-096's role-derived SELECT after REVOKE, but the actual tested fact is fn_my_permissions versus three metadata surfaces, not the effect of removing a direct grant. claims.summary: Azure SQL Entra authentication requires an identity-mapped SQL principal in the database. An authorized administrator can create that contained user; the existing Azure management role does not substitute for it.
SQL authentication is a supported alternative for password-based applications, but it abandons the required passwordless method and does not perform the requested Entra principal setup.
After user creation, the named object grant supplies the requested data access without broad database administration. Identity authentication and SQL authorization are distinct steps.
db_owner can supply broad database authority, appropriate for administration. It exceeds the stated Dispatch-only reading boundary and cannot replace creating the missing principal.

sourceReviews.supportingSummary: Inspected configuration steps, supported workload identities, Entra principals and Graph permissions. Azure SQL requires mapped SQL principals; SQL DB Contributor is management RBAC, not query authorization. Managed identity is passwordless, CREATE USER ... FROM EXTERNAL PROVIDER is supported, and the executing administrator needs SQL and, where applicable, Graph authority.

The unit demonstrates managed-identity database users created FROM EXTERNAL PROVIDER and separately granted SQL permissions. Its object-grant examples support choosing a specific table rather than its broad tutorial role memberships. I do not adopt the claim that identity credentials can never be stolen.

The SQL/Azure SQL GRANT syntax supports an object SELECT grant to a principal, while CONTROL/db_owner has broad database grant authority. The explicit no-inherited-grants-or-DENYs condition makes the requested object scope determinate without invoking the table-DENY/column-GRANT exception.

The managed identity already has a token but no target-database principal, so its Azure resource role alone cannot supply this mapping.

SQL username/password authentication is a real connection method described by the training, but substituting it would discard the expressly required passwordless identity and would not perform the requested Entra-mapped database setup.

After the mapped user exists, GRANT SELECT ON dbo.Dispatch TO that user supplies the narrowly requested read permission. Object GRANT is documented, and the question excludes conflicting/inherited permissions, so no whole-database role is needed for this object-only requirement.

db_owner is documented database-administrative authority, not a Dispatch-only read scope. It is appropriate for database administrators and requires an actual database principal; assigning it is neither a replacement for the missing mapping nor a least-privilege way to satisfy this request.

review.verificationNotes: The complete set is A,C. Network, token audience/validity and server Entra administrator are separated from the two missing SQL changes. Checked CREATE USER and object SELECT semantics without executing them. GA is appropriate for the Azure SQL managed-identity/principal/grant capabilities. Advanced is defensible for combining the management/data-plane distinction with independent identity creation and least-privilege object authorization, though the individual commands are not advanced syntax. Unlike archived direct-104's custom-role selection, creation of the Entra principal is indispensable here. PASS 2 only.
review.confidenceReason: High confidence from the explicit Azure SQL RBAC exclusion and mapped-user steps, corroborated by object GRANT evidence; no stored-secret or broad administrator shortcut is required.

The article expressly assigns SQL DB Contributor to management-related deployment operations, not database connectivity. It can be relevant for managing Azure resources but is not the removed Entra administrator property or a substitute for it.

review.verificationNotes: C is uniquely supported by the documented removal behavior, not inferred merely from a coincident outage. claims.summary: Retention preserves records that were captured and is relevant when existing events age out. These failed Entra authentications never reach the database, so retaining SQL audit data longer does not create their records.

Object SELECT auditing captures database data-access activity. It is useful for investigating reads after connection but cannot capture a failed authentication that never accessed the database.

sourceReviews.supportingSummary: Inspected Overview, auditing limitations and Remarks. It directs failed Entra-login investigation to the Entra admin center, contrasts SQL credential verification, and says successful connections are audited for both. The Remarks section says these failed Entra authentications do not access the requested database, so longer retention cannot manufacture their absent SQL audit records; it would help only with captured records aging out.

The article explicitly directs failed Microsoft Entra login investigation to the Microsoft Entra admin center because credentials are verified before database access. This is the stated rejection boundary, rather than an unhealthy SQL audit destination.

SQL auditing can select categories of database actions, and table SELECT auditing is useful for database reads. It cannot observe a sign-in that never reaches the database; narrowing capture to SELECT does not change that boundary.

The source distinguishes successful logins, which reach the database and can be audited, from failed Entra authentication before access. Successful records are useful for following accepted sessions, not evidence of the stipulated rejected sign-in.

claims.summary: The file-audit documentation recommends reduced permissions on copied archive files: administrator read/write and reader read. Active service access remains on the active destination, not on the independent archive.
The Application event log is a supported audit target, but authenticated Windows users can read and write it. It can suit less restrictive logging, not this tightly restricted archive.

The service needs read/write access to the active file destination. Retaining that write access on the independent archive defeats the stated separation, even though it is appropriate on active audit files.

The documentation recommends a separate reporting instance with access limited to audit administrators/readers. This reduces exposure through the production database engine without claiming all powerful administrators become unable to tamper.

sourceReviews.supportingSummary: Inspected Target and Permissions. Active binary-file ACLs allow service read/write, audit-administrator read/write and reader read; after copying to an archive the recommended ACLs are reduced to the audit administrator/reader groups. Separate audit-only reporting instances are recommended. Windows Application log access is broad; SQL CONTROL SERVER can access engine-readable files, and SQL Server 2022 also has VIEW SERVER SECURITY AUDIT for reading via fn_get_audit_file.

choiceReviews.rationale: The Target section explicitly recommends reducing a copied archive's ACLs to audit-administrator read/write and audit-reader read. Removing the production database-service grant from the archive while preserving its active-file access matches the requested independent write boundary.

The Windows Application event log is a supported audit destination on Windows, but the article warns that any authenticated user can read and write it. Default access is therefore a valid lower-restriction logging context, not this audit-team-only archive.

Service read/write is documented for the active audit file destination. Retaining it on the independent archived copies defeats the specified archive restriction; closed-copy 'repair' is not a documented reason to preserve production-service write access there.

The article recommends generating reports on a separate SQL Server instance accessible only to audit administrators/readers to reduce unauthorized access to audit records. That is the independent reporting boundary requested, with reporting-file access configured for the authorized audit team rather than broad production principals.

review.verificationNotes: Independently derive A,D. Active collection, copied archival storage and reporting access were evaluated as distinct locations/principals. The reporting instance still requires authorized read access to its input; the choices do not require the production service to lose active-file write access or assert absolute tamper-proofing.
